02 · Quantification

Detection probability curve, protein roll-up, detection filter, normalisation

Half of a DIA matrix is empty, and fainter precursors go missing more often. dpc() fits that as a curve, and dpcQuant() uses it to give every protein a value in every sample without imputing anything. This stage follows limpa’s vignette sequence.

Missingness

plotAveVsMis(y)

A downward trend means detection depends on intensity and the DPC has something to fit. A flat cloud would mean missingness is closer to random, where limpa still works but gains less over simpler methods.

The curve

dpcest <- dpc(y$E)
plotDPC(dpcest)
dpc_parameters <- tibble(
  intercept = dpcest$dpc[1],
  slope = dpcest$dpc[2]
)
round(dpc_parameters, 3)
intercept slope
-8.958 0.488

dpc() defaults to model = "cn" and its help says it then returns dpcCN(), the complete-normal estimator the limpa FAQ recommends for noisy data. Its subset = 2000 default fits on a systematic sample stratified by missingness and mean intensity rather than all 47,133 rows. limpa documents robust as “Only used if `model=‘on’”, so it does nothing here and the subsample supplies the robustness.

The fit comes out at 0.488, below the 0.7-to-0.9 band the FAQ calls typical for DIA-NN searched with match-between-runs, though inside the 0.1-to-1.0 range it calls usable. The vignette notes the slope comes out low when peptides vary a lot, which a within-subject design with heavy missingness might produce.

Quantification therefore uses the preset 0.7 that limpa’s FAQ suggests: “If dpcCN() doesn’t give a value in that range, it would be reasonable to run dpcQuant() with a preset value dpc.slope=0.7.” The fitted value is carried into a sensitivity run at the end.

The FAQ says a slope set too low makes the analysis more conservative. On this data the reverse held when it was last measured: the lower fitted slope gave smaller standard errors and more hits than the preset. The preset remains the documented setting and, here, the cautious one.

Note

The visual fit is not diagnostic. plotDPC() draws a curve in unobserved intensity against proportions computed on observed intensity, so some discrepancy is structural. Judge the slope.

Roll-up

dpcQuant() fits an additive precursor-plus-sample model per protein, maximising a posterior that scores observed values by squared residual and missing values by their DPC probability. The returned $other$standard.error is why this project uses limpa: dpcDE() reads it as a precision weight, so a protein reconstructed largely from missing precursors gets a wide standard error. Handing $E to lmFit() discards that and treats every protein as equally reliable.

That takes about 100 minutes, so it lives in a_script/02_quantify_run.R rather than here. This notebook loads what the script wrote, so a render doesn’t begin a long run by accident. Rerun the script by hand when the precursor matrix changes.

if (!file.exists(primary_file)) {
  stop(
    "No dpcQuant checkpoint. Run:\n",
    "  Rscript 01_Preprocess/02_Quantification/a_script/02_quantify_run.R"
  )
}
proteins <- readRDS(primary_file)$object

3,451 protein groups from 47,133 precursors. The matrix has no missing values; what varies is each value’s standard error.

Detection filter

filterByDetection() runs after dpcQuant() and before DE, and returns a logical vector. For a small experiment the help suggests setting n.samples to the smallest group size. Here that is BFR_T2 with 32 samples, one short because S06_L_T2 is missing.

The function counts detections across all samples and keeps a protein when that count clears the threshold, so the smallest group size sets a cohort-wide bar rather than guaranteeing detection within any one group.

group_sizes <- table(proteins$targets$group)
keep <- filterByDetection(proteins, n.samples = min(group_sizes))
proteins <- proteins[keep, ]

group_sizes

 BFR_T1  BFR_T2 HLRT_T1 HLRT_T2 
     33      32      33      33 
c(before = length(keep), kept = sum(keep), dropped = sum(!keep))
 before    kept dropped 
   3451    3042     409

Measured on an earlier run, the dropped proteins had a mean SE of 1.56 against 0.66 for those kept, and 0.15 detected precursors per sample against 7.48, so the typical sample measured nothing at all for them. Relaxing the threshold to limpa’s default of 3 recovered 371 of them, of which exactly one reached BH < 0.05 in any contrast, while the larger test set tightened the BH threshold enough to push 14 and 29 previously significant proteins back above 0.05 on the two training contrasts.

Normalisation

limpa places normalisation after dpcQuant() and before dpcDE() and performs none itself, because DIA-NN has usually normalised the precursors already. Normalised precursors do not make a normalised protein roll-up.

A single per-sample shift fixes the spread in per-sample medians but not the MA curve width, which cyclic loess may help with. Comparing a sample against the average of all samples gives a difference per protein, and fitting that against abundance gives a curve. A flat curve means the sample disagrees by a constant. A curve that travels means the disagreement depends on abundance. Both are reported before and after.

ma_width <- function(E) {
  a <- rowMeans(E)
  apply(E, 2, \(x) diff(range(lowess(a, x - a, f = 0.5)$y)))
}
spread <- function(E) diff(range(apply(E, 2, median)))

before <- c(ma_width = median(ma_width(proteins$E)), median_spread = spread(proteins$E))
unnormalised <- proteins$E
proteins$E <- normalizeBetweenArrays(proteins$E, method = "cyclicloess")
after <- c(ma_width = median(ma_width(proteins$E)), median_spread = spread(proteins$E))

round(rbind(before, after), 3)
       ma_width median_spread
before    0.448         1.175
after     0.161         0.430

The top row shows every sample’s intensity density before and after. The bottom row shows the sample whose curve travelled furthest before normalisation, against the average of all samples.

worst <- which.max(ma_width(unnormalised))
par(mfrow = c(2, 2))
plotDensities(unnormalised, legend = FALSE, main = "Before cyclic loess")
plotDensities(proteins$E, legend = FALSE, main = "After cyclic loess")
plotMD(unnormalised, column = worst, main = paste(colnames(unnormalised)[worst], "before"))
plotMD(proteins$E, column = worst, main = paste(colnames(proteins$E)[worst], "after"))

The curvature is unrelated to treatment or timepoint, so cyclic loess is not absorbing the effect being tested. proteins.rds is written after this step and is the matrix the model is fitted to.

WarningThe standard errors stay on the old scale

Cyclic loess remaps $E non-linearly and leaves $other$standard.error untouched. After normalisation the stored errors describe the unnormalised scale, and dpcDE() reads them as though they described the new one. Smyth recommends quantile or cyclic-loess normalisation of limpa protein quantifications when sample differences are technical (Bioconductor support, 2026).

What survives

protein_quality <- tibble(
  protein = rownames(proteins),
  gene = proteins$genes$Genes,
  n_precursors = proteins$genes$NPrec,
  prop_observed = proteins$genes$PropObs,
  mean_log2 = rowMeans(proteins$E),
  mean_standard_error = rowMeans(proteins$other$standard.error),
  mean_n_observations = rowMeans(proteins$other$n.observations)
)
summary(protein_quality[c("mean_log2", "mean_standard_error", "prop_observed")])
   mean_log2     mean_standard_error prop_observed    
 Min.   :12.98   Min.   :0.03107     Min.   :0.03716  
 1st Qu.:16.07   1st Qu.:0.38500     1st Qu.:0.30245  
 Median :17.10   Median :0.58428     Median :0.42324

NPrec is what the installed version writes; the help page calls it NPeptides. A protein with a high mean standard error and few observations is one whose estimate is drawn from DPC.

Points are coloured by participant, and the variance each factor explains in the leading dimension is below the plot. 32 of 33 participants contribute all four cells, so between-participant variation dominates; the participant term in the design removes it. Check any sample sitting far from its own participant. No group structure is expected here.

mds <- plotMDSUsingSEs(proteins,
  pch = 16,
  col = as.integer(factor(proteins$targets$participant))
)
r2 <- function(f) summary(lm(mds$x ~ factor(f)))$r.squared
round(c(
  participant = r2(proteins$targets$participant),
  group = r2(proteins$targets$group)
), 3)
participant       group 
      0.515       0.027

Slope sensitivity

Quantification is repeated against the fitted curve and compared with the primary run, with the same detection filter and normalisation applied to both. The primary run passes dpc.slope = 0.7 and lets limpa fit the rest, while the sensitivity run hands dpcQuant() the whole curve dpc() estimated, intercept included. dpcDE() reads the standard errors as precision weights, so whichever run carries the larger mean standard error is the more conservative setting.

The median absolute difference in protein abundance follows the table. It measures how far values move, not whether that movement survives a contrast: every comparison here is within one participant, so a shift common to a participant’s samples cancels out.

sensitivity <- readRDS(sensitivity_file)$object
sensitivity <- sensitivity[filterByDetection(sensitivity, n.samples = min(group_sizes)), ]
sensitivity$E <- normalizeBetweenArrays(sensitivity$E, method = "cyclicloess")

shared <- intersect(rownames(proteins), rownames(sensitivity))
tibble(
  slope = c(0.7, round(dpcest$dpc[2], 3)),
  role = c("primary", "sensitivity"),
  n_proteins = c(nrow(proteins), nrow(sensitivity)),
  n_shared = length(shared),
  mean_standard_error = round(c(
    mean(proteins$other$standard.error[shared, ]),
    mean(sensitivity$other$standard.error[shared, ])
  ), 3)
)

round(median(abs(proteins$E[shared, ] - sensitivity$E[shared, ])), 4)

This section renders only when c_data/quant_runs/proteins_slope_fitted.rds is present, since computing it costs about another 100 minutes. To produce it once:

Rscript 01_Preprocess/02_Quantification/a_script/02_quantify_run.R --sensitivity

After that it loads as the primary run does.

Refitting the contrasts under each slope is separate and not done here; the counts produced are recorded in this stage’s README.
